detailed_sections.full_notes: Large numbers are used to express large quantities such as populations, distances in astronomy, and financial budgets. In the Indian numbering system, values are grouped as Thousands (1,000), Lakhs (1,00,000 = 10^5), and Crores (1,00,00,000 = 10^7). In the International system, grouping is done in thousands, Millions (1,000,000 = 10^6), and Billions (1,000,000,000 = 10^9). Conversion relation: 1 Million = 10 Lakhs, 1 Crore = 10 Millions.

margin_notes.title: Population Comparisons
margin_notes.content: To compare populations of cities like Patna and Mumbai, we express them in lakhs/crores and find the scaling factor by division.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Shortcut techniques accelerate multiplication: To multiply a number by 5, divide the number by 2 and multiply by 10 (e.g., 116 * 5 = (116 / 2) * 10 = 58 * 10 = 580). To multiply by 25, divide the number by 4 and multiply by 100 (e.g., 824 * 25 = (824 / 4) * 100 = 206 * 100 = 20,600).

margin_notes.title: Shortcut Practice
margin_notes.content: Evaluate 464 * 5 and 312 * 25 using division shortcuts.

detailed_sections.full_notes: When integers are written sequentially (1, 2, 3, 4, ..., 9, 10, 11, ...), single-digit numbers occupy 9 positions. Two-digit numbers (10-99, 90 numbers) occupy 180 positions. Three-digit numbers (100-999, 900 numbers) occupy 2700 positions. Determining the n-th written digit requires calculating cumulative digit counts.

margin_notes.title: 1000th Digit Position
margin_notes.content: The first 9 digits come from 1-9. Digits 10 to 189 come from 10-99. The remaining digits come from 3-digit numbers starting at 100.

detailed_sections.full_notes: An arithmetic expression is a combination of numbers and operational signs (+, -, *, /). Expressions are separated into terms by addition and subtraction signs. For example, in 4 + (100 / 2), the terms are 4 and (100 / 2). Evaluating terms first simplifies reading and solving complex expressions.

margin_notes.title: Terms and Brackets
margin_notes.content: Brackets group quantities together so they can be treated as a single term inside a larger expression.

detailed_sections.section: 2.2 Algebraic Properties of Addition and Multiplication
detailed_sections.full_notes:
1. Commutative Property of Addition: a + b = b + a. Changing order does not change the sum.
2. Associative Property of Addition: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). Grouping does not alter the sum.
3. Distributive Property of Multiplication over Addition: a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c.

Subtracting a number is equivalent to adding its additive inverse: a - b = a + (-b). When removing brackets preceded by a minus sign, the sign of every term inside the bracket reverses: -(a + b) = -a - b and -(a - b) = -a + b.

margin_notes.title: Token Model
margin_notes.content: Using positive and negative integer tokens, subtracting a positive token is equivalent to adding a negative token.

detailed_sections.full_notes: When 1 unit is divided into 10 equal parts, each part is one-tenth (1/10 or 0.1). When one-tenth is divided into 10 equal parts, each part is one-hundredth (1/100 or 0.01). Place values to the right of the decimal point are Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.

margin_notes.title: Decimal Point
margin_notes.content: The dot '.' separates whole units on the left from fractional place values on the right.

detailed_sections.full_notes: A number like 3.47 equals 3 ones + 4 tenths + 7 hundredths = 3 + 4/10 + 7/100. Money conversion: 1 Rupee = 100 Paise, so 1 Paise = ₹0.01. Length conversion: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 mm = 0.1 cm; 1 m = 1000 mm, 1 km = 1,000,000 mm.

Adding and subtracting decimals requires aligning decimal points vertically so identical place values (ones, tenths, hundredths) are operated together. Equivalent decimals (0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200) allow filling trailing zeros for alignment.

margin_notes.title: Alignment
margin_notes.content: Always align the decimal points before adding or subtracting.

detailed_sections.full_notes: A letter-number (variable) represents an unspecified number or quantity that can change. Expressions formed with letter-numbers generalize relations. Examples: Shabnam's age = Aftab's age + 3 (s = a + 3). Perimeter of regular shapes: Equilateral Triangle = 3s, Square = 4s, Regular Pentagon = 5s.

margin_notes.title: General Formulas
margin_notes.content: Formulas allow concise, universal description of geometric and arithmetic rules.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Terms containing the exact same letter-numbers are like terms (e.g., 5y and 2y; -5g and -20g). Like terms can be combined by adding or subtracting their coefficients: 5y + 5y + x + x = 10y + 2x. Unlike terms cannot be combined.

margin_notes.title: Simplification
margin_notes.content: Simplify p + p + p + q = 3p + q.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Algebraic rules describe growing patterns:
1. Matchstick squares: 1 square = 4 sticks, 2 squares = 7 sticks, w squares = 3w + 1 sticks.
2. Folded rope cuts: Cutting a rope folded r times yields r + 1 (or 2^r + 1) pieces.
3. Endless 4-column grid: Number in row r, column c = 4(r - 1) + c.

margin_notes.title: Grid Formula
margin_notes.content: In a 4-column grid, row r column c value is given by 4r - 4 + c.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Two distinct lines on a plane intersect at at most one point. When two lines intersect, four angles are formed. Key properties:
1. Vertically Opposite Angles are equal: angle a = angle c and angle b = angle d.
2. Linear Pairs: Adjacent angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees (supplementary): angle a + angle b = 180, angle b + angle c = 180.

margin_notes.title: Uniqueness of Intersection
margin_notes.content: Two non-coincident straight lines can never intersect at more than one point.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Parallel lines lie in the same plane and never intersect, no matter how far extended in either direction. The perpendicular distance between parallel lines is constant throughout. Perpendicular lines intersect at right angles (90 degrees).

detailed_sections.full_notes: Folding a square paper in half creates a crease parallel to top/bottom edges. Subsequent parallel folds double the number of parallel line segments created. Folding perpendicular to horizontal creases forms a grid of right angles.

margin_notes.title: Crease Patterns
margin_notes.content: Horizontal folds produce parallel creases; vertical folds produce perpendicular creases.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Parity refers to whether an integer is Even or Odd.
Rules:
1. Even + Even = Even; Odd + Odd = Even; Even + Odd = Odd.
2. Even * Anything = Even; Odd * Odd = Odd.
Representation: Any even number = 2n; Any odd number = 2n - 1 (or 2n + 1).

margin_notes.title: Loose Sheet Parity
margin_notes.content: Sum of page numbers on a loose sheet from a book (pages 2k-1 and 2k) is always ODD.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Magic Square: An n x n grid filled with distinct integers where every row, column, and diagonal has the same sum. For a 3x3 grid using numbers 1-9, magic sum = 15, and central cell must be 5. Cryptarithm: Alphabetic puzzle where letters represent distinct digits.

margin_notes.title: 3x3 Magic Square

chapters.chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

detailed_sections.full_notes: When three lines intersect pairwise in a plane at three distinct points, they form a triangle. The three points of intersection are vertices, and the line segments connecting them are sides.

margin_notes.title: Direct vs Roundabout Path
margin_notes.content: The direct straight path between two points is always shorter than any roundabout path passing through a third point.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Triangle Inequality Theorem: A triangle can exist if and only if the sum of the lengths of ANY two sides is strictly GREATER than the length of the third side.
Mathematical conditions for side lengths a, b, c:
1. a + b > c
2. b + c > a
3. c + a > b
Shortcut test: The sum of the two smaller side lengths must be strictly greater than the largest side length.

margin_notes.title: Quick Existence Check
margin_notes.content: Can sides be 3 cm, 3 cm, 7 cm? No, because 3 + 3 = 6 < 7.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
1. Equilateral Triangle: All three sides equal (a = b = c). An equilateral triangle of any positive side length always exists because a + a = 2a > a.
2. Isosceles Triangle: Two sides equal.
3. Scalene Triangle: All three sides unequal.

margin_notes.title: Equilateral Always Exists
margin_notes.content: For any side length s > 0, s + s = 2s > s is always true.

scripted_dialogues.speaker: Teacher
scripted_dialogues.speech_text: The sum of the two smaller sides must strictly exceed the longest side.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Brahmagupta's Formula for Multiplication of Fractions (628 CE):
(a / b) * (c / d) = (a * c) / (b * d).
To multiply fractions, multiply numerators together and denominators together.

margin_notes.title: Historical Roots
margin_notes.content: Indian mathematician Brahmagupta formally stated rules for fraction operations in 628 CE.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal (multiplicative inverse):
(a / b) / (c / d) = (a / b) * (d / c) = (a * d) / (b * c).
Quotient Behavior:
1. Dividing by a fraction between 0 and 1 results in a quotient GREATER than the dividend (e.g., 8 / (1/4) = 32 > 8).
2. Dividing by a number > 1 results in a quotient LESS than the dividend.

margin_notes.title: Division Effect
margin_notes.content: Dividing by a proper fraction enlarges the value!

margin_notes.title: Telescoping Cancellation
margin_notes.content: Intermediate numerators and denominators cancel out completely.

scripted_dialogues.speaker: Aaron

scripted_dialogues.speaker: Teacher
scripted_dialogues.speech_text: Brahmagupta's ancient reciprocal multiplication rule elegantly solves sharing problems.
